author: Crispus Nyaga
title: Is Dropbox Worth $9 Billion? - Dropbox (NASDAQ:DBX)
text:
Thesis
Dropbox ( DBX ) was one of the largest tech IPO this year. The company went public in March raising more than $756 million. On the inaugural day, the stock opened at $21 valuing the company at more than $12 billion. As of this writing, the company’s stock is trading at $22 giving it a market valuation of slightly above $9 billion. While I love the company’s original product, I am sceptic about the current valuation, even after the YTD 20% decline.
Introduction
Dropbox was started in 2007 by Andrew Houston and as of November, the company had more than 500 million users from around the world. It has more than 12 million paying users, which is higher than the 11 million users it reported in its S1 report. Over the years, the company has sought to transform itself from a mere cloud storage to a team collaboration company. It has done this by launching products like DropBox Paper and Showcase . Its goal is to create a unified platform for storage, collaboration, project management, and professional sharing.
To be clear, while I am skeptical about Drobox, this article does not recommend shorting the stock. This is because in the past, we have seen stocks of highly unprofitable SAAS companies rise as investors focus on the non-GAAP metrics like the user growth. Indeed, the SAAS industry is one of the most expensive sectors with investors paying higher PE multiples. For example, companies like Box ( BOX ), Veeva Systems ( VEEV ), Zendesk ( ZEN ), and Hubspot ( HUBS ) have forward PE ratios of 896, 51, 192, and 118 respectively.
Challenge #1: Users
Dropbox was among the first companies to bring cloud storage to the masses. After launching in 2007, the company has managed to attract more than 500 million users. Using its innovative marketing model, the company was able to keep sales and marketing expenses lower than that of its ‘peers’. For example, in 2017, the company spent only 28% of its revenue on sales and marketing. In comparison, Box, Carbonite ( CARB ), and Zendesk ( ZEN ) spent 56%, 37%, and 51% of their revenues on S&M.
The reason I put an apostrophe on the peers is that Dropbox has no real publicly traded peers. While the storage service is similar to that of Box, the two companies have a very different user base. This is because most of its users are individuals. The majority of Box users are corporate clients. Therefore, valuing Dropbox as an ordinary SAAS company is difficult because very few subscription companies target individuals. Writing for Bloomberg, Shira Ovide said:
It’s a consumer software company with a side gig of software sales to businesses.
The challenge for Dropbox is on how to continue adding more paying users. This will be difficult because the cloud storage industry has become more competitive with all the major companies like Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Alphabet ( GOOG ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ) having their own products. Critics of this argument will say that DBX has continued to add more users despite these companies having their competing products. They are right. However, individuals are very different from corporations who can stick with a product for a long time. Recent research show that they are more price sensitive and more likely to switch to other less expensive products.
This is the main reason that made our company switch from Dropbox to Microsoft Onedrive early this year. Before that, we were each using Microsoft Office 2016 and storing our documents in Dropbox. Every month, we were spending $82 for a DBX plus subscription. Since we are a small company, we started looking for a cheaper alternative. We tried Google Drive – now Google One – but decided to settle for Onedrive for one major reason. Microsoft charges us $7 a month (or $70 a year) on Microsoft 365 package that comes with free 1 terabyte of free storage.
Today, cost-sensitive users will most likely prefer paying $7 a month for Microsoft 365 or $10 for a Google One subscription. This is already happening as the company has started experiencing slower premium user growth.
Challenge #2: Business Users
As mentioned above, most of DBX users are individuals. In its S1, the company said that it had more than 300K business teams customers. It also said that approximately 56% of all Fortune 500 companies had at least one Business Team within the organization. In contrast, Box claims that 69% of all Fortune 500 companies have signed up for its services.
Therefore, because of challenge #1, Drobox will have the challenge on how to add more business clients. This will be harder because of the products that it currently has that will justify more companies to join or switch from other companies. Dropbox has three main products. The first is the core storage product. Dropbox Paper is was launched in 2017 to help teams collaborate. To date, while official numbers have not been released, Paper – which is free – has not been a wide success. This is probably because users already have alternative collaboration products like Google Docs and Box Notes . The other product is Showcase that allows users to ‘ present their work to clients and business partners through a customizable, professionally branded webpage.’
True, DBX has partnered with other companies like Adobe ( ADBE ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), IBM ( IBM ), and SAP. However, it will be difficult for DBX to convince businesses to switch to its platform from other companies with such limited capabilities. Challenge #3: Valuation
As mentioned above, DBX has more than 12 million users from around the world. The company has benefited from the internet penetration in the developed and emerging markets. At the current valuation of more than $9 billion, investors believe that each paying user is worth ~$750. This is lower than when it launched its IPO. Then, each user was worth ~1080. In the last earnings call, the company said that its ARPU increased to $118.60 , which it attributed to ‘strong adoption of our premium professional and advanced plans by new paying users.’ By dividing the value of each user to the ARPU, we get that investors are paying ~6X its value today.
In 2017, DBX generated revenues of more than $1.10 billion. This year, the company is expected to generate $1.386 billion. In 2019 and 2020, the company is expected to generate $1.60 billion and $1.83 billion respectively. In the third quarter, the company’s revenue growth was 25.6%, which was the lowest in years. Projecting DBX revenues is relatively easy. For example, if ARPU remains at $118 and the company doubles its users, it will generate revenues of $2.8 billion. Even if you give it a net profit margin of 30% - similar to MSFT -, it will take time to justify the current valuation.
Challenge #4: Acquisition Target?
In September, Marius Swart argued that DBX was a strong acquisition target. In the article, he pointed that potential acquirers would be CRM, AAPL, MSFT, and GOOG. To me, this idea does not make sense. First, CRM has build its business around corporations. Therefore, it will make little no sense to acquire a company that creates software for individuals. A Box acquisition would make more sense.
AAPL has iCloud that is similar to DBX and one that helps it boost its ecosystem. I don’t see how DBX will create value for AAPL. The same is true with MSFT and GOOGL.
Takeaway
Dropbox is currently valued at more than $9 billion. The loss-making company will remain being a consumer-facing software company because bigger companies like MSFT and GOOG have a first-mover advantage on products that DBX is launching like Paper and Showcase. It is impossible to see how the company will continue adding users as the industry becomes saturated. Therefore, I can’t see how the company’s $9 billion valuation can be justified considering that the user growth is starting to slow down. However, as I mentioned above, DBX is a story stock and for some time, investors will not focus on the key GAAP fundamentals. Instead, they will focus on metrics like ARPU and the total number of customers added. This makes shorting the stock relatively difficult especially for investors with a short-term horizon.
 long BOX, MSFT, AAPL.
